1.1: 1.1 Argument. Likewise he writes to Timothy about exhortation to martyrdom, and about every rule of truth, and what will be in the last times, and about his own passion, writing to him from the city of Rome. Paul an apostle. First the Apostle greets, then gives thanks for the good which he has, where he shows his desire to see him. Afterwards he admonishes him to preach, and to patience in martyrdom, by his own example and in other ways. Then he says what sort of men there will be in the last days: finally of the imminent time of his own dissolution. By the will of God. Not by my merits, as if he said: Likewise you also were sent freely, and therefore are the more bound to preach grace.
1.3: 1.3 I give thanks. He gives thanks for his good, commending the grace of the faith which is in Christ. Remembrance. For Timothy wept when dismissed by Paul, ready to go with him to all dangers. What therefore he had when present, let him hold when absent, receiving also the remembrance of the faith that may admonish you, since it was firm even in women.
1.6: 1.6 For which cause. His faith being commended, he exhorts him to preach it without fear and shame. By the imposition of hands. That is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, which you received for the establishing of the Church, for working miracles, for every service of religion.
1.7: 1.7 Of fear. Peter, disturbed by fear, denied Christ. Hence: Do not fear those who kill the body, Matthew 26. We have not received the spirit of this fear, but of that of which the Lord says: Fear him who can destroy both body and soul in hell. For the Holy Spirit gives fear not of the world but of God, who can destroy in the hell of fire.
1.8: 1.8 Be not therefore. He teaches that constancy is to be had, and that one is not to be ashamed in the profession: for there is no reason to be ashamed of it: because although Christ was seen as man, yet by his deeds he appeared God; and though he was crucified, yet he rose from the dead, and in the sight of many, a cloud receiving him, he ascended into heaven. Where therefore weakness is supposed, there power appears.
1.9: 1.9 Who has delivered us. It is fitting to repay him who delivers: since we cannot worthily answer his benefits, let us at least faithfully and earnestly carry out his embassy.
1.10: 1.10 Who has destroyed. Death, as conquered, is not to be feared for the faith of Christ. He has enlightened. To what end these things look, there he opens: Having the form. Through the Gospel. God has shown incorruptible life, which was before unknown, shown, I say, through the preaching of the Gospel of which Paul is the preacher.
1.11: 1.11 Whereunto I am appointed. Here he exhorts by his own example. Preacher, and apostle, and teacher, etc. What reason is there, since he continually calls himself teacher of the Gentiles? Doubtless he wishes to persuade that the Gentiles also are called to the inheritance of God, and therefore are not to be repelled from the fellowship of the faith.
1.12: 1.12 For I know. As if he said: Therefore I am not confounded, that is I do not fail, or I do not suffer in vain, because he promised and is truthful and powerful: and therefore I have believed him himself, who will repay me. Because he is able. He is secure by the hope and magnificence of the Savior, because what he commits to him is safe. He commits to him his salvation, that here suffering for him he may find salvation with him when he begins to judge, that punishing the unfaithful he may pronounce this one worthy of eternal life.
1.13: 1.13 Hold the form. Here he shows to what end the aforesaid things regarding himself look. As if he said: So I labor in this office entrusted to me: likewise therefore you also, holding the form, etc. Of whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes. These pretended to be with the Apostle in order to find calumny: but after they saw themselves exposed, they withdrew from him.
2.4: 2.4 No man being a soldier. As if he said: If you wish to be a good soldier, do not entangle yourself in secular business, because no man, etc. Business. Secular business is when the mind is occupied with the care of gathering money without labor of body, like merchants and the like: which lest he do, because being weak he could not labor, he forbids.
2.6: 2.6 The husbandman that laboreth. As if Timothy asked: Whence then shall I live, since I cannot dig, and am ashamed to beg? he adds the husbandman that laboreth. As if he said, though you are not entangled in secular business, there is yet whence you can live: Because it behooves, etc. First to partake. That is, to take. Of the fruits. That is the necessaries from the hearers, because the laborer is worthy of his hire; as the husbandman or vinedresser first tastes the first fruits of his labor, so the Apostle bids him who is first take, and so distribute to the rest. For he ought first to supply his own need from what he has received, and afterwards minister to others from what remains.
2.8: 2.8 Be mindful. Labor as I do, and this in hope of eternal life. He mentions these things not for Timothy's sake, but for the sake of the heretics whom he foresaw would come and deny them.
2.9: 2.9 As an evildoer. Here he notes the insult which was heaped upon him. But the word of God is not bound. As if he said: Though therefore I am bound in body, yet the word of God is not bound: I who do not cease to teach those present by speech, and those absent by letters.
2.10: 2.10 Salvation, etc., with glory, etc. As if he said: You are justified that here you may obtain salvation, and after this life heavenly glory.
